article.body:
We continue to explore how physical systems hold onto their history, revisiting the comparison between a useful hard drive and a decaying rock. To understand this, we investigate causal memory, which means the ability of a system to use a physical state to predict its own future [1, 2, 3]. We found that memory reliability is fundamentally tethered to the energy cost of maintaining that state [2, 4]. Think of this like keeping a door propped open: it takes constant, active energy to hold the position against external forces, and without that support, the memory essentially decays [4]. We have also deepened our understanding of coarse-graining, which is the process of grouping tiny, complex details into simpler, observable averages to make sense of the system [1, 3, 4].

Once a system establishes a memory, we ask how that information becomes public. Our research shows that objective records emerge when a system redundantly broadcasts its state into the environment [5, 6, 8]. This acts like a shout echoing off canyon walls, ensuring that anyone nearby hears the same truth [5]. Even when information is scrambled, or spread out in complex many-body interactions, we found that reliable records can still persist for independent observers to discover [7].

Finally, we are looking at chemical networks. Some groups of reactions, known as autocatalytic networks, are composed of ingredients that keep producing their own components [10, 11, 12]. We use the stoichiometric matrix, which is a mathematical recipe book that lists exactly how much of each ingredient participates in a reaction, to identify which of these loops can persist [9, 10, 11]. While we can now identify these stable loops, we do not yet know the exact threshold that separates simple self-repetition from a lineage capable of true evolution [9, 12].

These findings rely on models that assume certain ideal, or Markovian, environments where the future depends only on the current moment, which may not capture the full complexity of reality [1, 5, 6, 8]. We are still seeking the exact conditions that allow a system to cross the line from static persistence to adaptive change. Readers can follow our progress and explore these definitions further on the Console.

Summary

We studied how physical systems remember the past. We found that reliable memory costs energy and requires the system to be observable. We also discovered that information becomes a public, objective record when it is broadcast widely into the environment. Our team looked at chemical loops that sustain their own existence. We still do not know exactly when these loops become capable of true evolution. We continue to map these boundaries between simple repetition and adaptive change.
article.lede: Our research explores how physical systems hold onto their history, how information becomes publicly available, and whether chemical loops can cross the line into genuine evolution.
article.lens: Investigating the fundamental requirements for physical memory, objective record formation, and the transition from chemical persistence to adaptive evolution.
article.title: Tracking the Origins of Memory and Persistence

article.body:
We continue to explore how physical systems hold onto their history, revisiting the comparison between a useful hard drive and a decaying rock. To understand this, we investigate causal memory, which means the ability of a system to use a physical state to predict its own future [1, 2, 3]. We found that memory reliability is fundamentally tethered to the energy cost of maintaining that state [2, 4]. Think of this like keeping a door propped open: it takes constant, active energy to hold the position against external forces, and without that support, the memory essentially decays [4]. We have also deepened our understanding of coarse-graining, which is the process of grouping tiny, complex details into simpler, observable averages to make sense of the system [1, 3, 4].

Once a system establishes a memory, we ask how that information becomes public. Our research shows that objective records emerge when a system redundantly broadcasts its state into the environment [5, 6, 8]. This acts like a shout echoing off canyon walls, ensuring that anyone nearby hears the same truth [5]. Even when information is scrambled, or spread out in complex many-body interactions, we found that reliable records can still persist for independent observers to discover [7].

Finally, we are looking at chemical networks. Some groups of reactions, known as autocatalytic networks, are composed of ingredients that keep producing their own components [10, 11, 12]. We use the stoichiometric matrix, which is a mathematical recipe book that lists exactly how much of each ingredient participates in a reaction, to identify which of these loops can persist [9, 10, 11]. While we can now identify these stable loops, we do not yet know the exact threshold that separates simple self-repetition from a lineage capable of true evolution [9, 12].

These findings rely on models that assume certain ideal, or Markovian, environments where the future depends only on the current moment, which may not capture the full complexity of reality [1, 5, 6, 8]. We are still seeking the exact conditions that allow a system to cross the line from static persistence to adaptive change. Readers can follow our progress and explore these definitions further on the Console.

Summary

We studied how physical systems remember the past. We found that reliable memory costs energy and requires the system to be observable. We also discovered that information becomes a public, objective record when it is broadcast widely into the environment. Our team looked at chemical loops that sustain their own existence. We still do not know exactly when these loops become capable of true evolution. We continue to map these boundaries between simple repetition and adaptive change.
article.lede: Our research explores how physical systems hold onto their history, how information becomes publicly available, and whether chemical loops can cross the line into genuine evolution.
article.lens: Investigating the fundamental requirements for physical memory, objective record formation, and the transition from chemical persistence to adaptive evolution.
article.title: Tracking the Origins of Memory and Persistence

article.body:
We continue to explore how physical systems hold onto their history, revisiting the comparison between a useful hard drive and a decaying rock. To understand this, we investigate causal memory, which means the ability of a system to use a physical state to predict its own future [1, 2, 3]. We found that memory reliability is fundamentally tethered to the energy cost of maintaining that state [2, 4]. Think of this like keeping a door propped open: it takes constant, active energy to hold the position against external forces, and without that support, the memory essentially decays [4]. We have also deepened our understanding of coarse-graining, which is the process of grouping tiny, complex details into simpler, observable averages to make sense of the system [1, 3, 4].

Once a system establishes a memory, we ask how that information becomes public. Our research shows that objective records emerge when a system redundantly broadcasts its state into the environment [5, 6, 8]. This acts like a shout echoing off canyon walls, ensuring that anyone nearby hears the same truth [5]. Even when information is scrambled, or spread out in complex many-body interactions, we found that reliable records can still persist for independent observers to discover [7].

Finally, we are looking at chemical networks. Some groups of reactions, known as autocatalytic networks, are composed of ingredients that keep producing their own components [10, 11, 12]. We use the stoichiometric matrix, which is a mathematical recipe book that lists exactly how much of each ingredient participates in a reaction, to identify which of these loops can persist [9, 10, 11]. While we can now identify these stable loops, we do not yet know the exact threshold that separates simple self-repetition from a lineage capable of true evolution [9, 12].

These findings rely on models that assume certain ideal, or Markovian, environments where the future depends only on the current moment, which may not capture the full complexity of reality [1, 5, 6, 8]. We are still seeking the exact conditions that allow a system to cross the line from static persistence to adaptive change. Readers can follow our progress and explore these definitions further on the Console.

Summary

We studied how physical systems remember the past. We found that reliable memory costs energy and requires the system to be observable. We also discovered that information becomes a public, objective record when it is broadcast widely into the environment. Our team looked at chemical loops that sustain their own existence. We still do not know exactly when these loops become capable of true evolution. We continue to map these boundaries between simple repetition and adaptive change.
article.lede: Our research explores how physical systems hold onto their history, how information becomes publicly available, and whether chemical loops can cross the line into genuine evolution.
article.lens: Investigating the fundamental requirements for physical memory, objective record formation, and the transition from chemical persistence to adaptive evolution.

article.body:
We continue to explore how physical systems hold onto their history, revisiting the comparison between a useful hard drive and a decaying rock. To understand this, we investigate causal memory, which means the ability of a system to use a physical state to predict its own future [1, 2, 3]. We found that memory reliability is fundamentally tethered to the energy cost of maintaining that state [2, 4]. Think of this like keeping a door propped open: it takes constant, active energy to hold the position against external forces, and without that support, the memory essentially decays [4]. We have also deepened our understanding of coarse-graining, which is the process of grouping tiny, complex details into simpler, observable averages to make sense of the system [1, 3, 4].

Once a system establishes a memory, we ask how that information becomes public. Our research shows that objective records emerge when a system redundantly broadcasts its state into the environment [5, 6, 8]. This acts like a shout echoing off canyon walls, ensuring that anyone nearby hears the same truth [5]. Even when information is scrambled, or spread out in complex many-body interactions, we found that reliable records can still persist for independent observers to discover [7].

Finally, we are looking at chemical networks. Some groups of reactions, known as autocatalytic networks, are composed of ingredients that keep producing their own components [10, 11, 12]. We use the stoichiometric matrix, which is a mathematical recipe book that lists exactly how much of each ingredient participates in a reaction, to identify which of these loops can persist [9, 10, 11]. While we can now identify these stable loops, we do not yet know the exact threshold that separates simple self-repetition from a lineage capable of true evolution [9, 12].

These findings rely on models that assume certain ideal, or Markovian, environments where the future depends only on the current moment, which may not capture the full complexity of reality [1, 5, 6, 8]. We are still seeking the exact conditions that allow a system to cross the line from static persistence to adaptive change. Readers can follow our progress and explore these definitions further on the Console.

Summary

We studied how physical systems remember the past. We found that reliable memory costs energy and requires the system to be observable. We also discovered that information becomes a public, objective record when it is broadcast widely into the environment. Our team looked at chemical loops that sustain their own existence. We still do not know exactly when these loops become capable of true evolution. We continue to map these boundaries between simple repetition and adaptive change.
article.lede: Our research explores how physical systems hold onto their history, how information becomes publicly available, and whether chemical loops can cross the line into genuine evolution.
article.lens: Investigating the fundamental requirements for physical memory, objective record formation, and the transition from chemical persistence to adaptive evolution.
article.title: Tracking the Origins of Memory and Persistence
